newsitem.title: USA: Brazil asset slump seen as corrective--US analysts.
newsitem.headline: Brazil asset slump seen as corrective--US analysts.

text.p: Recent Asian currency instability may have sent shivers through Brazil's bond and stock markets, but U.S. analysts said Tuesday the slump could be taken as the inevitable unwinding of a strong rally.
Talk had swirled that the effective devaluation of the Thai baht and Philippine peso might pressure Brazil financial assets, and by Monday asset prices began to crumble.

In the late U.S. morning Tuesday, the liquid Brazilian "C" bond BR8D14=RR sank 5/8 to 81-1/4 bid. Brazil stocks sank 6.02 percent in moderate turnover, as the Bovespa index .BVSP was down 765 points to 11,933 points.
But analysts saw the moves as a natural correction.

"This is the first opportunity people have had to take profits through the first half of July," said John Welch, chief Latin America economist at Paribas. "You're getting a little bit of a panic correction. This is going to pass."

Thailand, weighed down by a massive current accounts deficit, implemented an effective delavuation of its baht earlier this month. The Philippines last week allowed similar measures for its peso. Brazil's current account deficit, overvalued currency and high domestic debt burden made it vulnerable to market rumors of potential contagion from Asia.
But analysts said the country's outlook remained stable.

"At this stage it's a healthy warning but not with the strength yet to have either systemic or contagion effects of substance," said Paulo Leme, senior international economist at Goldman, Sachs and Co Inc.
One portfolio manager at a major U.S. emerging market fund described the move as an inevitable unwinding of easy money that had pumped emerging debt prices to record highs.
"There was too much speculation, too much easy money," the investor said. "The market is to blame to the extent that it whips us into a speculative frenzy."

The portfolio manager said the Brazilian government needed to stem the instability by assuring markets it would meet any concerns about the currency or domestic debt by adjusting interest rates to stem any flight.
Brazil's central bank said Tuesday that the Sao Paulo bolsa exhibited a "normal" technical reaction and that it would not alter exchange rate policy under any circumstances.

U.S. analysts said Brazil's situation had not changed, that the country still faced an overvalued real, onerous domestic debt burden, and current account deficit that had widened to 4.2 percent of GDP.
"Make no mistake that Brazil's current account deficit and external financing needs make it a natural candidate for traders to reasses the situation more closely than other Latins," Leme said.
"It's a healthy warning that countries that have large external financing needs are vulnerable to the humors of the markets," he added.
